title: Bending the Rules
tagline: playing with idioms, and the garbled forms to avoid
why: Native speakers twist idioms on purpose for humour, headlines and emphasis, and they also garble them by accident. Knowing the difference lets you enjoy wordplay, avoid embarrassing errors and judge when a fixed phrase is better left alone.
know: correct forms: for all intents and purposes, a moot point
understand: a twist needs a well-known original
able: spot and correct garbled idioms in speech and writing
extend or twist a metaphor deliberately for effect
decide when not to use an idiom at all
mistakes: For all intensive purposes, the deal is done.
For all intents and purposes, the deal is done. A classic mishearing, known as an eggcorn.
We'll burn that bridge when we come to it.
We'll cross that bridge when we come to it. Mixing in burn your bridges is only funny on purpose.
Ironically, it rained on the day of our picnic.
Unfortunately, it rained on the day of our picnic. Bad luck isn't irony; irony needs a reversal of expectation.
The new policy gives managers free reign.
The new policy gives managers free rein. From riding: loose reins, not a king's reign.
(Cover letter) I'm a team player who thinks outside the box and hits the ground running.
Replace stacked cliches with specifics: name a result you achieved. Too many idioms in formal writing sound empty.
bigidea: Idioms are fixed, but not frozen. Natives bend them for effect: headline writers love puns, such as grate expectations for a story about a cheese shop, and comedians extend a familiar image until it becomes absurd. The trick works only because everyone knows the original.

Accidental bending is different. A mixed metaphor joins two images that clash (we'll burn that bridge when we come to it). A malapropism swaps in a similar-sounding wrong word (a mute point). Some speakers turn this into a style: the baseball player Yogi Berra became famous for odd but memorable sayings, now nicknamed Yogi-isms.

Finally, many metaphors are dead: nobody notices that a deadline or the foot of a mountain is figurative. Writers can revive a dead metaphor by taking it literally. George Orwell warned against what he called dying metaphors in between: worn-out images that people use to avoid thinking.
hidden: The foot of the mountain was covered in fog.
Traffic hit a bottleneck near the bridge.

expressions.example: For all intents and purposes, the election was over by nine o'clock.
expressions.bend: Fixed: don't change it, but British English often says to all intents and purposes. Commonly misheard as for all intensive purposes.
expressions.note: Slightly formal and wordy. In concise writing, effectively or in practice is often better.

expressions.meaning: stop something at an early stage
expressions.example: If a new hire is rude to customers, nip it in the bud on day one.
expressions.bend: The object can change (nip the problem in the bud); nip and bud are fixed.
expressions.note: The garble nip it in the butt is a real error and a popular joke. The image is pinching off a flower bud.

expressions.meaning: a question that no longer matters, or one still open to debate
expressions.example: Whether we should have hired more staff is a moot point now that the shop has closed.
expressions.bend: Fixed: moot, never mute. Also the point is moot.
expressions.note: In North America it usually means irrelevant; in British usage it can still mean debatable. Context decides.

expressions.example: Honestly, I couldn't care less who wins the cooking show.
expressions.bend: Many Americans say I could care less with the same meaning. It's common but widely criticised; use couldn't in careful speech.
expressions.note: Can sound rude. Softer options: I'm not too bothered or it doesn't really matter to me.

expressions.meaning: an example that proves what you have just said
expressions.example: Small towns are losing their banks; case in point, ours closed in March.
expressions.bend: Fixed. Also a case in point. Often misheard and written as case and point.
expressions.note: Used right after a general claim. For example is neutral; case in point sounds more pointed and argumentative.

expressions.meaning: obey the rules or official policy, often reluctantly
expressions.example: Backbench MPs were told to toe the line on the budget vote.
expressions.bend: Tense and noun vary: toed the party line. Often misspelled tow the line.
expressions.note: The image is runners with their toes on a starting line. Orwell noted the tow spelling as proof that writers no longer picture the image.

expressions.meaning: move steadily towards a target; focus closely on something
expressions.example: The investigators quickly homed in on the accounting department.
expressions.bend: Tense varies: homing in on, homed in on. Hone in on is widespread in North America but many editors still mark it as an error.
expressions.note: The image is a homing pigeon or missile. Hone means sharpen, as in hone your skills.

expressions.meaning: complete freedom to act as you choose
expressions.example: The new chef was given free rein to redesign the menu.
expressions.bend: Fixed noun: give someone free rein, have free rein. Spelled rein, not reign.
expressions.note: From riding: a horse given loose reins can go where it likes. The reign spelling is a very common written error.

culture.how: Orwell argued that tired, ready-made phrases let writers avoid thinking. His first rule tells writers to drop any figure of speech they have met many times in print and to find a fresh image or speak plainly instead. He also noticed that people mangle dying metaphors because they no longer picture them.
culture.ask: Is Orwell's rule realistic for everyday business writing? Which cliches would you ban first?
culture.find: George Orwell Politics and the English Language

culture.how: Mrs Malaprop constantly reaches for impressive words and picks slightly wrong ones that sound similar. She is so memorable that English named the mistake after her: a malapropism. Her name comes from the French mal à propos, meaning inappropriate.
culture.ask: Why do people misuse big words? Have you heard a funny malapropism in English or in your own language?

culture.how: Dogberry, a self-important constable, keeps choosing grand words that mean the opposite of what he intends, yet his bumbling night watch accidentally uncovers the villain's plot. Such errors are sometimes called dogberryisms.
culture.ask: Why might a writer let a foolish character solve the mystery? What does that say about cleverness and language?

culture.how: A nine-line riddle in which every line offers a different metaphor for the speaker, and the hidden answer is pregnancy. The form plays along: nine lines of nine syllables each, echoing nine months. It shows how stacking metaphors can be deliberate and clever, not mixed.
culture.ask: Try to describe yourself, your job or your city as a riddle of three quick metaphors. Can Bill guess it?

culture.how: The Ottawa-born singer lists a series of frustrating situations and calls them ironic. Critics and comedians famously pointed out that most are bad luck or bad timing rather than true irony, so the song became a favourite example in debates about what irony really means.
culture.ask: Describe a situation from your life or the news that is truly ironic, not just unlucky. What makes it ironic?

match.why: Intents means aims: for every purpose that matters.
Pinch off the bud and the flower never opens.

match.r: a question that no longer matters
match.why: In North America moot usually means irrelevant now.
It's impossible to care any less than I already do.
A case relevant to the point you are making.
Runners put their toes on the line and wait for the signal.
Like a homing pigeon finding its way home.
A rider loosens the reins and lets the horse choose its way.

sort.h: Is each phrase the correct form, a garbled word (malapropism or eggcorn), or a mixed metaphor blending two idioms?

items.why: The standard form: moot, meaning no longer relevant.
Correct: rein, as in horse riding.
Intensive replaces intents and: a mishearing.

items.w: we'll burn that bridge when we come to it
items.why: Blends cross that bridge with burn your bridges.

items.w: that's the way the cookie bounces
items.why: Blends the way the cookie crumbles with the way the ball bounces.
Blends rocket science with brain surgery.

items.w: wake up and smell the roses
items.why: Blends wake up and smell the coffee with stop and smell the roses.

pick.q: The merger hasn't been signed, but ___ the two firms already operate as one company.
pick.why: Correct form: for all intents and purposes, meaning in practice.

pick.q: Whether we should have booked earlier is ___; the flight is full anyway.
pick.why: A moot point: no longer worth discussing.

pick.q: Teachers were given ___ to design their own curriculum this year.
pick.why: Free rein: complete freedom, from horse riding.

pick.q: Fuel prices affect everything; ___, our grocery bill rose fifteen percent.
pick.why: Case in point: an example proving what you just said.

pick.q: Cabinet ministers who refuse to ___ may lose their posts.
pick.why: Toe the line: follow the rules or party policy.

pick.q: The search team ___ the signal from the lost hiker's phone.
pick.why: Home in on: move steadily toward a target.

pick.q: Frankly, ___ about the office party; I'll be on holiday anyway.
pick.why: I couldn't care less: I don't care at all.

pick.q: If staff start arriving late, ___ before it becomes a habit.
pick.why: Nip it in the bud: stop it at the start.

spot.q: The question of who pays is a mute point now that the event is cancelled.
spot.why: Moot means no longer relevant. Mute means silent.

spot.q: For all intensive purposes, the referendum result is final.
spot.why: A classic mishearing. The phrase is for all intents and purposes.

spot.q: The editor gave the young journalist free reign to cover the protests.
spot.why: Rein, as in a horse's reins: freedom to go where you like.

spot.q: Opposition members refused to tow the line on the pipeline bill.
spot.why: Toe the line: put your toes on the line, follow the rules.

spot.q: Prices in this town keep rising; case and point, a coffee now costs six dollars.
spot.why: Case in point: an example that proves your claim.

type.q: We'll cross that ___ when we come to it; let's focus on today.
type.why: Cross that bridge when we come to it: deal with a problem when it actually arrives.

type.q: That's the way the cookie ___, I'm afraid; we lost the contract.
type.why: That's the way the cookie crumbles: that's life, accept it.

type.q: The detectives slowly ___ in on the gang's leader.
type.why: Home in on (or zero, close in on): focus on a target. Honed in on is common in North America but disputed.

type.q: Honestly, I couldn't care ___ about celebrity gossip.
type.why: I couldn't care less: I don't care at all.

type.q: Whether the stadium should have been built is a ___ point; it opened last year.
type.why: A moot point: no longer worth discussing.

type.q: City inspectors want to nip the rat problem in the ___ before winter.
type.why: Nip it in the bud: stop it early.

bend.q: Which headline sounds like natural, deliberate wordplay? ___
opts: Bakers rise to the occasion as bread prices soar
Bakers ascend to the occasion as bread prices soar
Bakers rise on the occasion as bread prices soar
bend.why: Rise to the occasion stays intact, and rise also suggests bread dough: a pun only works on the real idiom.

bend.q: Which extended metaphor sounds natural and witty? ___
opts: We've opened a tin of snakes, and now the worms are organising.
We've opened a can of worms, and now the worms are organising.
We've opened a can of worms in the bud.
bend.why: Extending can of worms works because the original is untouched; the others mix images.

bend.q: Which deliberate twist sounds natural and witty? ___
opts: The early bird gets the cheese, but the worm gets the mouse.
The early birds catches the worms early.
The early bird gets the worm, but the second mouse gets the cheese.
bend.why: The joke keeps the original intact, then adds a clever twist about mousetraps.

bend.q: Which sentence suits a formal quarterly report? ___
opts: Sales fell sharply in the third quarter.
Sales went south big time, and it's a whole new ball game.
Sales fell off a cliff and hit rock bottom in the basement.
bend.why: In formal reports, plain language beats stacked idioms and mixed images.

talk: Orwell would ban any metaphor that you have met many times in print. Pick three cliches from your workplace or the news and replace each with a fresh image or plain words.
Alanis Morissette's Ironic is famous for situations that aren't strictly ironic. Describe one truly ironic situation from your life or the news.
Which English idioms did you mishear or misunderstand when you first learned them? What did you think they meant?
Role-play: Bill is your editor. Defend a mixed metaphor in your article as deliberate humour, or agree to fix it and explain how.
Mrs Malaprop and Dogberry use big words to sound important. Do people in your workplace use jargon the same way? Give examples.

match.r: two clashing images in one phrase
match.why: E.g. we'll burn that bridge when we come to it.

match.r: a wrong word that sounds like the right one
match.why: Named after Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's The Rivals.

match.r: a figure of speech nobody notices any more
match.why: E.g. the leg of a table or the head of a department.
Once fresh, now tired from repetition.
E.g. for all intensive purposes: the wrong words still make some sense.

match.r: a reversal of what is expected
match.why: A fire station burning down is ironic; rain on a picnic is just bad luck.

pick.q: Calling a simple task not rocket surgery blends two idioms; it's a ___.
pick.why: A mixed metaphor or blend: rocket science plus brain surgery.

pick.q: A fire station burning down is a classic example of ___.
pick.why: Irony: the opposite of what you'd expect happens.

pick.q: Grandpa told the doctor he had very close veins instead of varicose veins; it was a lovely ___.
pick.why: A malapropism: a similar-sounding wrong word.

pick.q: The committee agreed that the matter was ___ since the building had already been sold.
pick.why: A moot point: no longer relevant.

pick.q: Our new manager gives us ___ to choose our own hours.
My friend ___ who wins the election; she never votes.
pick.why: Couldn't care less: doesn't care at all.

spot.q: Let's nip this argument in the butt before dinner is ruined.
spot.why: Nip it in the bud: stop it early, like pinching off a flower bud.

spot.q: For all intense purposes, my phone is my office.
spot.why: The correct form is for all intents and purposes.

spot.q: We didn't get the grant, but that's the way the cookie bounces.
spot.why: Cookies crumble; balls bounce. Mixing them is a blend error.

spot.q: We'll burn that bridge when we come to it; first let's finish the budget.
spot.why: Cross that bridge when we come to it: deal with it later. Burn your bridges is a different idiom.

type.q: The premier told her caucus to ___ the line on the trade deal.
type.why: Toe the line: follow official policy.

type.q: We give our grandson free ___ to explore the garden all summer.
Rising rents are a case in ___: housing is the issue of this election.
type.why: A case in point: an example that proves the claim.

type.q: For all intents and ___, the old factory is a museum now.
type.why: For all intents and purposes: in every practical sense.

type.q: The vet quickly homed ___ on the cause of the dog's limp.
type.why: Home in on: focus on a target.

type.q: Whether the senator should resign is now a ___ point; she quit this morning.
type.why: A moot point: no longer relevant.

bank.q: ___, the strike is over; only the paperwork remains.
bank.why: For all intents and purposes: in practice, effectively.

bank.q: Parents were given ___ to plan the school fundraiser.
bank.why: Free rein: complete freedom, from loose reins on a horse.

bank.q: Team members who won't ___ will be moved to another project.
bank.why: Toe the line: follow the rules.

bank.q: The thermal camera ___ the missing child within minutes.
bank.why: Home in on: locate and move toward a target.

bank.q: Politicians rarely answer the question; ___, last night's debate.
bank.why: Case in point: an example that proves your claim.

bank.q: Whether we should have sold the house in spring is now ___.
bank.why: A moot point: no longer worth discussing.

bank.q: Teenagers often claim they ___ what their parents think.
bank.why: Couldn't care less: don't care at all.

bank.q: The supervisor decided to ___ before the gossip spread.
bank.why: Nip it in the bud: stop something early.

bank.q: That's the way the ___ crumbles; we'll try again next year.
bank.why: That's the way the cookie crumbles: that's life.

bank.q: Don't worry about the next stage yet; we'll ___ that bridge when we come to it.
bank.why: Cross that bridge when we come to it: deal with it later.

bank.q: Mrs Malaprop gave her name to the ___, a comic misuse of a similar-sounding word.
bank.why: A malapropism: named after Sheridan's character in The Rivals (1775).

bank.q: Saying we'll burn that bridge when we come to it produces a ___ metaphor.
bank.why: A mixed metaphor combines two clashing idioms.

bank.q: Orwell advised writers to avoid stale ___ and find fresh images instead.
bank.why: Orwell's first rule warns against figures of speech you are used to seeing in print.

bank.q: The new director has free rein to restructure the department.
bank.why: Correct: free rein, spelled like a horse's reins.

bank.q: My nephew could care less about hockey, which shocks his Canadian grandparents.
bank.why: Could care less is common informal US speech with the same meaning, but many see it as illogical. In careful or Canadian/British usage, say couldn't care less.

bank.q: Analysts are homing in on the cause of the market crash.
bank.why: Correct: home in on means focus on a target. Hone means sharpen.

bank.q: Rising crime is a case and point for more police funding, the mayor argued.
bank.why: The phrase is a case in point: an example that supports the claim.

bank.a: For all intents and purposes the deal is done.
alt: The deal is done for all intents and purposes.
bank.why: For all intents and purposes + main clause. A comma after purposes is optional in writing.

bank.a: Let's cross that bridge when we come to it.
alt: When we come to it let's cross that bridge.
bank.why: Cross that bridge + when we come to it.

bank.a: The new manager gave us free rein on the project.
alt: On the project the new manager gave us free rein.
bank.why: Give someone free rein on something.
